title: Fraud referrals, payment suspensions and the exceptions granted
question: By the State’s own account, how often did a fraud referral lead to charges, and how often were payments to a provider under suspicion stopped?
finding: The State told the federal agency it sent 408 credible-fraud referrals to the State fraud prosecutors in five review years; as of December 2025 charges had been filed on 34 of the 408 in its table, 13 ended in a judgment or restitution and 67 were declined. Over five years it imposed 97 payment suspensions and granted 339 exceptions not to suspend, all at the prosecutors’ request: for each suspension, 3.5 exceptions. Recoveries rose from $11.0 million in 2020-21 to $136.0 million in 2024-25. The federal letter of January 2026 says California is $1.60 billion of the $1.80 billion it is recouping from the eight jurisdictions with State-only programs.
how: Figures as printed in the State’s reply of 17 February 2026 (questions 3, 6 and 13) and the federal letter of 27 January 2026; the per-year referral table is copied row by row. The ratio of exceptions to suspensions is this project’s arithmetic.
limits: Prosecutors ask for an exception so that a suspect is not tipped off; the rules provide for an exception, and it can protect a case. The referral table is a point-in-time snapshot and later years have more cases still active. Nothing here is broken out for San Francisco; the reply names Los Angeles and other counties as where fraud cases concentrate, and names the San Francisco Health Plan only for a missing compliance-officer procedure in an audit.
